title: Muhammad Iqbal
hookLine: the poet-philosopher of South Asia who urged the self to rise

cards: A schoolyard in India. Children line up in the morning and sing a song that begins, in Urdu, with the claim that their land is better than all the world.
A wedding in Lahore, and someone recites a couplet about the falcon who refuses to build a nest. A seminar room, and a professor lectures on how the Qur'an speaks of the human self.
Three places, three audiences, one author: a poet who studied law and philosophy, wrote poetry in two languages, and kept asking what a human being is capable of. Today: Muhammad Iqbal.

teach.h: A POET IN URDU AND PERSIAN.
teach.b: Iqbal grew up in the Punjab, studied in Lahore, then in England and Germany. He came home a philosopher, a lawyer, and above all a poet, writing in Urdu and Persian.
His great word was khudi: selfhood, the self. Not selfishness. For Iqbal, khudi was the spark God placed in each person, meant to be strengthened, not dissolved.
He looked at Muslims under colonial rule and saw people who had learned to make themselves small: waiting, imitating, apologizing. His poetry kept saying the opposite. Rise.

teach.h: GOD ASKS: WHAT DO YOU WISH?
teach.b: One often-quoted couplet goes, in paraphrase: raise your selfhood so high that, before each turn of destiny, God himself asks the servant, tell me, what do you wish? Bold words, meant boldly.
But the self he praised is not a self without God. It grows strong by drawing near to God, the way a flame grows by being fed.
A bird he returns to again and again is the falcon, a creature of the high air that, in his verse, won't settle for an easy nest.

teach.h: SURELY WE CREATED MAN OF THE BEST STATURE.
teach.b: Behind this stands a line of surah at-Tin, in Pickthall's words: "Surely We created man of the best stature." Some readers hear Iqbal's idea in it: a dignity to grow into. Readers disagree about him, too.
Some hear a poet of spiritual courage. Others focus on his politics, or argue over how far his philosophy strays from the old scholars. Pakistan honors him, and his songs are still sung in India.

how: Iqbal's poems are recited and sung in Urdu and Persian at gatherings, in schools and in qawwali, and his lines are often quoted in sermons and speeches across South Asia.

o: a poet who urged the self to rise toward God
a Mughal emperor who wrote poems in Persian
the teacher who taught Abduh in Cairo

p: won't settle for an easy nest

s: khudi is selfhood: the spark God placed in each person, meant to grow strong by drawing near to God.
he wrote in Urdu and in Persian.
in his couplet, God asks the servant what he wishes
raise your selfhood so high that before each turn of destiny God asks: what do you wish?

games.q: you're a poet. the people around you have learned to make themselves small under foreign rule. what does your poetry tell them?
o: forget God and trust only yourselves.
rise: strengthen the self by drawing near to God.
games.why: Iqbal's khudi is a self that rises, and it grows strong by drawing near to God, not by leaving him.

practice: If there's a place in your life where you make yourself small, waiting for permission or apologizing for taking up room, bring it to mind.

Ask what rising would look like there, not shouting, just standing a little taller, and let one true, hopeful sentence form. If you pray, hold the words of surah at-Tin, of the best stature; if not, just hold your line.

wordCard.voice: Muhammad Iqbal. The poet-philosopher of South Asia who taught khudi, selfhood, and urged the self to rise toward God. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian and Urdu: selfhood, Iqbal's key word for the God-given self.

carryVoice: Your line: the self can rise. Khudi means selfhood, never selfishness. Stand tall; see you tomorrow.

sources.q: Surely We created man of the best stature
